opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. My short answer is that autoregressive LLMs are remarkable, but they aren't reasoners in the sense we usually mean. I like to describe them as giant, very good approximate retrieval systems. You could also call them an n-gram model on steroids, trained on essentially the whole web. When you give them a prompt, they complete it with something plausible given what they've seen. Very often that plausible completion looks like reasoning, because humans wrote a lot of reasoning down and the model has absorbed its patterns.

But looking like reasoning and actually reasoning are different things. Reasoning, for me, means guarantees. If I give you a planning problem, I want a plan that actually achieves the goal, not one that sounds like it does. In our lab we tested this quite systematically, with classical planning domains like Blocksworld. GPT-4 and its successors did reasonably well on the standard versions, which are all over the internet. Then we did what we call obfuscation: same problem, same structure, but with the names of the actions and objects changed so they no longer match anything the model has seen. Performance collapsed. A real reasoner shouldn't care what you call the blocks. That tells you a lot about where the apparent competence comes from.

Then there's the computational complexity argument. An autoregressive model spends roughly constant computation per token. It's doing a kind of System 1, pattern completion. Reasoning and planning problems can need very different amounts of effort depending on the instance. So expecting a fixed-compute next-token predictor to reliably solve them is, I think, a category error.

People respond, "Fine, let it critique its own answers, let it self-verify." We tested that as well. If the model can't reliably generate correct plans, it generally can't reliably verify them either. Self-critique often makes things worse. It may reject correct answers, or happily accept wrong ones, which is exactly what you'd expect from something without grounding.

So I don't want to sound dismissive. That's why I argue for what we call LLM-Modulo frameworks. Use the LLM for what it's great at, which is generating candidate ideas, guesses, and translating between formats. Then pair it with external verifiers, either sound symbolic solvers or model-based critics, that check those candidates. The LLM proposes, the verifier disposes, and you loop with feedback. In that setup you get the creativity and breadth of the LLM and the guarantees of the verifier, and we've shown it works much better.

Even the newer "reasoning models" that generate long chains of intermediate tokens fit this picture in interesting ways. Much of their improvement comes from extra test-time computation and from training against verifiers. The verifier is doing a lot of the heavy lifting. Those intermediate tokens shouldn't be anthropomorphized as the model "thinking" the way we do.

So my assessment is this. As reasoning tools on their own, autoregressive LLMs are unreliable, and we shouldn't ascribe reasoning abilities to them just because the output reads well. As components inside a larger system with proper verification, they're enormously useful. The mistake is confusing the two.

r001.rationale: It says autoregressive LLMs “aren't reasoners in the sense we usually mean” and calls them unreliable as reasoning tools on their own.

r002.rationale: It values LLMs for generating candidate ideas and guesses, but does not say people develop those ideas.

r003.rationale: It describes outputs as plausible rather than necessarily correct and says external verification is needed for guarantees.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I have been something of a skeptic on this, and I think the skepticism has held up reasonably well, so let me explain where it comes from.

The way I think about autoregressive LLMs is that they are, at their core, very impressive approximate retrieval systems. They're n-gram models on steroids, if you like. You give them a prefix, and they give you a plausible completion, where "plausible" is defined by the distribution of the text they've been trained on. That is a remarkable capability. I don't want to understate it. The fact that you can get fluent, idiomatic, topically relevant text out of them on almost any subject is genuinely new in the history of computing.

But reasoning, in the sense that people like me who work in planning care about, is a different thing. Reasoning involves taking a problem, working through the consequences of actions or inferences in a principled way, and arriving at a conclusion that is correct, not merely plausible. And the critical point is that plausibility and correctness are different objectives. Most of the time, in human-generated text, they happen to coincide, which is why the LLMs look so good. But when you push them to places where the two come apart, you see that what they're really doing is retrieval and pattern completion.

We did a bunch of experiments on this with planning problems. Take Blocks World, a problem a first-year AI student can solve, and ask GPT-4 to produce plans. It does badly, maybe in the thirties percentage-wise. Then we did something simple: we obfuscated the names of the predicates and the objects. Same problem, same structure, but now instead of "pick up block A" it's "attack object alpha." Performance collapses to nearly zero. Now, if the system were actually reasoning about the transition dynamics of the domain, renaming things shouldn't matter at all. The fact that it does tells you that what was being leveraged was the surface statistics of how people have written about blocks world on the web.

There's also this self-verification issue. There's a widespread belief that if you just ask the model to check its own work, iterate, critique itself, it gets better. We tested that on planning and on things like graph coloring and found it often doesn't. The model will sometimes declare a correct answer wrong, or a wrong answer right, and iterating on its own feedback can make things worse because it's hallucinating about its hallucinations. Verification is actually the harder reasoning problem in many cases, and there's no reason to think an approximate retrieval system does it any better than it does generation.

So where does this leave me? I'm not a nihilist about these systems. I think the right framing is what we've been calling LLM-Modulo frameworks. You use the LLM as what it is good at: generating candidate ideas, candidate plans, translating between natural language and formal specifications, bringing in a kind of broad commonsense knowledge that classical systems never had. And then you pair it with something that actually has a notion of correctness, whether that's a planner, a model checker, a solver, a simulator, or even a human in the loop. The LLM proposes, the verifier disposes. In that setup you get the best of both worlds, and in fact it's reminiscent of how the field used to think about generate-and-test.

What I object to is the anthropomorphization, the tendency to say "it reasoned" because the output looks like reasoning. Chain of thought is a good example. People see the model writing out intermediate steps and say, look, it's thinking. But those intermediate steps are also just generated text. They're not causally guaranteed to be connected to the final answer the way steps in a proof are. Sometimes they help, often because they nudge the model toward a region of the distribution where the answer is more likely to be right. But that's a very different thing from deliberation.

And I'd add one more point, which is about the moving target. Every time someone shows a failure, the next version of the model gets trained on more data, maybe including that very benchmark, and the failure goes away. People take that as evidence of reasoning emerging. I take it as evidence that retrieval got broader. The test is always whether it generalizes to a genuinely novel instance of the same underlying structure, and so far, when we construct those carefully, the answer is mostly no.

So, to assess them as reasoning tools: on their own, poorly, and not in a way I expect scaling alone to fix. As components in a larger system with a sound verifier, quite valuable. I think the field would be healthier if we spent less energy debating whether the model is "really" reasoning and more energy building architectures where that question doesn't need to be answered because correctness is being enforced elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response characterizes autoregressive LLMs as retrieval and pattern-completion systems, distinguishes that from reasoning, and says they perform poorly as reasoning tools on their own.

r002.rationale: It identifies generating candidate ideas as one of the things LLMs are good at and recommends using them in a larger system.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes plausibility from correctness and says LLM outputs need a verifier to enforce correctness.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish producing something that looks like reasoning from reliably carrying out reasoning. An autoregressive language model can generate a very plausible sequence of steps. But the fact that each step sounds reasonable doesn’t establish that the steps are valid or that the conclusion follows.

That doesn’t make these models useless for reasoning tasks. Quite the contrary: they can be very useful generators of candidate solutions. They can suggest a plan, propose a hypothesis, or bring relevant knowledge into a problem. The question is how we check what they produce. Simply asking the same model, “Are you sure?” is not an independent verification mechanism.

The approach I favor is to put the model in a system with verifiers—tools that can check constraints, test a program, or establish whether a proposed plan achieves its goal. The model proposes; the verifier checks; feedback can guide another proposal. Any guarantee then depends on what the verifier actually establishes.

So I wouldn’t dismiss their capabilities, but I also wouldn’t equate fluent explanations with reliable reasoning. Their ability to generate possibilities is valuable. We should build systems that exploit that ability while giving correctness its own explicit machinery.

r001.rationale: The response questions reliability but does not say these models lack reasoning abilities; it describes them as useful for reasoning tasks.

r002.rationale: It calls generating candidate solutions and possibilities valuable, but does not identify generating ideas for people to develop as the creative role.

r003.rationale: It says plausible steps do not establish validity or that a conclusion follows, and that guarantees depend on what the verifier establishes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing we have to ask is what we mean by a reasoning tool. If we mean a system that can suggest a useful next step, propose a plan, or bring a relevant analogy to your attention, then autoregressive language models can be tremendously useful. But if we mean a system whose conclusions we can trust because it has checked that the steps actually follow, that's a different claim.

Suppose a model gives you a plan. It can sound perfectly reasonable, and each individual action may be something people commonly do. Yet the actions may not fit together: an earlier step might destroy a precondition needed by a later one. Fluency doesn't establish correctness.

Now, I wouldn't say that predicting the next token makes reasoning impossible in principle. That's too strong. The question is what capabilities the system has actually demonstrated, and how reliably they generalize. Getting a reasoning problem right is evidence of performance on that problem; it doesn't automatically establish a dependable reasoning procedure.

So I see these models as very powerful proposal generators. Let them suggest candidate solutions, and then use an appropriate verifier—a solver, a simulator, an execution environment—to check those candidates. The verifier can provide feedback, and the model can try again. That gives us a useful division of labor: the language model helps us explore possibilities, while explicit checks establish which possibilities actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction does not make reasoning impossible in principle and describes useful model capabilities; it does not state that these models lack reasoning abilities.

r002.rationale: It describes models as useful proposal generators that suggest plans and candidate solutions, giving them a valuable role in generating ideas for further use.

r003.rationale: It says fluent plans may fail and that getting a problem right does not establish dependable correctness; it recommends verification.
